Takebacks
Accepts
Takebacks per game. While you play, ↶ Take back sits beside Offer draw and Resign: it undoes your last move, and the bot's reply if it has made one. The clocks carry on as they are. Set to Never, the button doesn't appear. On Lichess the same setting answers the opponent's takeback requests; once they are used up, it declines and says so in the chat.
Draws & desperation
Accepts draw offers
Accepts your ½ offer unless it thinks it's clearly ahead — judged at its own rating. Repetitions too: it steps out of one it wouldn't accept as a draw
Accept margin200 cp
Accepts when its perceived advantage is at most this many centipawns. Perception = engine eval blurred to the bot's rating — a 700 misjudges by ±200 cp, a 2400 barely at all. Clock-aware: never accepts while you're about to flag (it's playing for the win on time), and gets far more agreeable when it's the one about to flag. Declines are wordless, like a human's. The same terms decide a threefold repetition: a move that would let the game be drawn by one (its own, or a reply it leaves you) is played only if it would take that draw; otherwise it plays something else.

The bot works down each column, with either step on or both: the opening repertoire plays the lines you tick (shares sum to 100%), the main line plays the database's most popular move from wherever the game stands, and the engine plays the rest. Opponent clock under
Premoves once you drop under this, to keep your clock burning and play for the flag — the aggressive reason humans premove. 0 = off.
Bot clock under
Premoves once the bot drops under this, out of its own time desperation. 0 = off. Either trigger alone is enough to start premoving.
Premove rate
Of the moves that clear the confidence bar below, the percent the bot actually premoves — not a percent of all moves. 100% = premoves every time it's confident.
Min confidence
Only premoves when Maia is at least this sure of your reply — humans premove on near-forced replies, not coin flips. 95%, the default, keeps it to replies that are all but forced, as a human premoves; dropping it far below ~60% makes the bot premove into positions a human never would, and its play will look erratic.
Busted-premove delay
Seconds of extra thinking when you bust a premove — the "didn't see that coming" stall. This is your reward for springing a trap: the bot burns its own clock. 0 = no penalty. Never allowed to flag the bot.
Requires Maia 3. A premove is worked out while you think, so it plays at the rating and temperature the time-pressure curves give for 5 s, and must pass the CP Budget and Hard Floor like any other move — if the engine can’t check it, the bot thinks normally instead. This game: none yet.

Time–rating model
ELO(s) = ELO₀ + D(s) − D(anchor)
D(s) = 339 − 1442·s−0.283
s = think seconds per move · anchor = base/60 + increment
Halving think time ≈ −100 ELO at rapid pace, steeper in blitz
Degradation curve based on fit shown by IM Professor Kenneth Regan describing ELO as a function of time-control, during his Perpetual Chess Podcast interview with Ben Johnson.
How time pressure simulation works
The bot simulates a rated player under time pressure using two complementary mechanisms:
▸ ELO reduction — Full credit to Professor Regan for his work, full blame to me for extrapolating his data-based findings based on full games under different time controls to this unsubstantiated estimation of ELO drop for individual moves under different time constraints. Maia is called at a lower ELO as think time shrinks under time pressure: full ELO at the time control’s nominal pace (base/60 + increment seconds per move), degrading below it following the curve shown above. Every point is draggable if you want a shape different from the formula, and Match Regan model puts them all back on it — the Max ELO drop slider caps how deep the curve goes, so at its default the curve stops short of the model in faster time controls
▸ Temperature escalation — ELO stays fixed but sampling temperature rises as think time shrinks, flattening Maia's move probabilities toward uniform without ever reordering them: a near-forced move stays the near-certain pick, while a genuine toss-up becomes far less predictable (instinctive, less creative play — typical of a strong player with no time to calculate). A quick engine check ensures a degraded pick never improves on Maia's top choice. How far up the curve the bot actually goes is set by Calm ↔ Panicky in Personality: at 0 it follows the curve as drawn (mild by default — Max temp 2), toward Calm it rises less, fully Calm leaves the temperature untouched, and fully Panicky rises 2.5× as fast.
▸ Only when time is really short — both curves describe a bot being forced to move faster than it would like. With Fixed interval or Instantaneous timing the pace is a number you set, not something the clock forced, so neither curve runs. Complexity scaled (From the clock) budgets from the clock and uses them; so does Mirror user, which plays at your pace — when you speed up under time pressure it speeds up with you, and degrades the way you do. Premoves are worked out while the opponent thinks, and play at the rating and temperature these curves give for 5 s.
Each curve has its own ON/OFF toggle next to its title, so you can run either mechanism alone, both together, or switch both off for constant strength regardless of clock.
How Bot Behavior Works
Move timing, quality degradation, and move selection pipeline
Reference
Move selection pipeline — order of operations
1
THINK TIME — calculated first, drives everything downstream
Think time per move is computed before the engine is queried. It combines the timing mode (pace, complexity-scaled, fixed, mirror), the Hustle attractor (fast +5 → slow −5 multiplier on base time), clock-pressure shortcuts (weaponizer, clock-mirror), and a ±20% jitter. This produces an actual think time in seconds that is then fed into both degradation curves — not a clock average. A hustler thinking 0.3 s sees heavy degradation; an overthinker thinking 12 s sees almost none.
2
ENGINE QUERY — Maia ELO degraded by think time (curve A)
Maia3 is queried at an ELO that curve A maps from the computed think time. Long think → ELO stays near target. Short think → ELO drops, producing the move distribution of a lower-rated player. The result is a probability for every legal move reflecting what a human at that (possibly degraded) rating would actually play.
3
SAMPLING TEMPERATURE — margin-aware softening keyed on think time (curve B)
Curve B maps the same think time from step 1 to a sampling temperature T, ramping from the Engine panel's base Temperature (comfortable think time) up to the Max temp slider's ceiling (default 8, minimal think time). Raising T flattens Maia's probabilities toward uniform (p^(1/T)) WITHOUT reordering them — a near-forced move (e.g. 99% vs 1%) stays dominant even at the ceiling, while a close call (e.g. 41% vs 40%) flattens fast. That is the point of softening by temperature rather than by a rank cutoff: pressure scales with how contested the position already is, not with an arbitrary window width. The Day Lower / Upper sliders still define a static percentile band (unaffected by think time); Luck shifts that band toward higher- or lower-probability moves without changing its width.
4
MIN-PROBABILITY FILTER — absolute popularity floor
Any move below the absolute minimum probability (the "Exclude lowest %" slider) is discarded. This is a pure distribution control — real centipawn protection happens at step 7, with actual engine evals rather than probability as a stand-in.
5
ATTRACTOR REWEIGHTING — per-move probability boosts
Each eligible move is simulated on a scratch board and scored against every active attractor slider. Result: p′ = p × exp(Σ logBoost). Attractors stack multiplicatively. CP Budget controls total magnitude — at 0 cp all attractors are silent.
Piece type — boosts moves by selected piece
Trade seeker — boosts captures + threats created
Space Cadet — boosts moves that reduce bot's weak squares (full board; discoveries + blocks counted)
Fort Knox — boosts moves that increase friendly coverage
Gambito — boosts ECO gambit continuations in opening
Attacker — boosts moves that increase pieces threatened
Structure — boosts pawn moves that tighten/loosen islands
Pawn strategic — flat boost to all pawn advances
6
TEMPERATURE SAMPLING — weighted random draw
Each reweighted probability is raised to p^(1/T), then one move is drawn proportionally. T < 0.15 → always picks the top move; T = 1.0 → unmodified Maia distribution; T > 1 → flattened toward uniform. Curve B (step 3) ramps T from the base Temperature up toward the Max temp slider's ceiling (default 8) as think time shrinks, scaled by the Panicky pressure setting — a steady personality barely raises T even at 0s left, a panicky one reaches the ceiling well before then. The Coffeehouse Hustler personality overrides T with a phase curve instead: T = 5.0 in the opening (many pieces), fading to T = 0.6 in the endgame.
7
CP BUDGET ACCEPTANCE — real engine check
Runs only when attractors reshaped the distribution and the sampled pick differs from Maia's most-popular move. One shallow Stockfish probe evaluates the pick, the most-popular move, and the next few personality favourites. The pick is played only if it loses ≤ CP Budget versus the most-popular move; otherwise the bot walks down its preference order, falling back to the most-popular move itself. This is what makes the Centipawmeter real centipawns — probability is never used as a stand-in for move quality.
Think time feeds move quality — not just pacing
Think time is the central input to both degradation curves. Controls that shorten think time — the Hustle slider, the Weaponizer, clock-mirroring, the Blink shortcut — all reduce move quality through curves A and B, not just move speed. A bot configured to think 0.3 s per move will have its ELO degraded and its move pool narrowed to first-pass instinctive choices on every move, exactly as a human would under severe time pressure.
Think time — order of precedence
These are checked in order, and the first one that applies wins — the timing mode is consulted only if nothing above it fired:
1 · Premove — if a premove is armed and still legal it fires instantly, bypassing think time entirely.
2 · Instantaneous mode — returns 0.
3 · Time Weaponizer — opponent under the trigger: play at the minimum move time.
4 · Move blink — near-forced position (entropy < 0.5): 200–500 ms.
5 · Timing mode — fixed / mirror / complexity-scaled / pace, then the human modifiers, familiarity decay and jitter.
Because blink sits above the mode, leaving it on with Fixed interval would let obvious recaptures ignore the duration you set — so selecting Fixed switches blink off and marks the row. You can switch it back on if you want that behaviour.
Premove simulation
Human speed-chess players premove: they queue a reply before the opponent has moved, and it fires the moment the opponent's move lands. It saves seconds but commits blind — which is what makes it exploitable.
The bot reproduces this in two Maia passes, run while you are on move so it never blocks you:
1 · Predict your move from the current position. If Maia's confidence is under Min confidence, it doesn't commit.
2 · Apply that predicted move and ask what it should play in the resulting position — and lock that answer in.
When you move, the locked reply fires instantly whatever you actually played. If your move made it illegal, the premove is busted: the bot must think from scratch and pays the Busted-premove delay off its own clock. That is the reward for springing the trap — and the reason to bait one.
Min confidence is the setting that matters most. At 85% the bot only premoves on near-forced replies, as humans do. Far below ~60% it premoves into positions no human would, and play looks erratic rather than fast. Premove rate is a percentage of the moves that already cleared that confidence bar, not of all moves. The low-clock gate is optional and has two independent triggers — the opponent's clock or the bot's own — and either alone is enough to arm one.
Requires the Maia 3 model, since the prediction runs on it. Premoving is reported in the collapsed Move Timing header, because a bot replying instantly looks like a malfunction if you don't know it's switched on.
BOT CREATION & PLAY REFERENCE TECHNICAL BRIEF
Every control, formula and pipeline stage. Opens in a new tab — use your browser's Print → Save as PDF for an offline copy.
Premoves & premove traps
What's a premove?

In fast chess, players premove — queueing a reply before the opponent has moved, so it fires the instant their clock starts. With premoving on, the bot asks Maia what you're most likely to play, if it assesses that your reply is forced, it applies that supposedly forced move, chooses its own next move based on that position — then commits to it.

Which engine answers?

Both halves of the guess come from Maia 3, not Stockfish. Maia is trained on human games, so it predicts what a player would do rather than what is objectively best — which is what makes a premove worth trapping. It runs twice: once on the current position to guess your reply, and again on the resulting position to choose the bot's own answer.

Maia is asked at the bot's own rating band, not yours. A human premoving is also guessing from their own understanding, so a strong bot anticipates a weaker opponent imperfectly — exactly as a strong human would.

Premoving is inert until the Maia 3 model has been downloaded; the bot simply plays normally instead. Download it in the vs Bot panel.

What's a premove trap?

A premove saves seconds, but commits blindly. A premove trap is the counter: work out what your opponent has queued, then play the move that makes their committed reply the wrong one.

The premove doesn't react to you. It fires whatever you played, so the bot can walk past free material — playing its queued move elsewhere while a piece it would normally capture sits there untouched. Squares that look unsafe often aren't, once you notice the defender is busy playing something it decided on before you moved.

If your move makes the premove illegal — pinning the piece, capturing it, or moving its target away — the premove is busted instead, and the bot must think from scratch, burning the Busted-premove delay on its own clock.

See it played

Worked examples are easier to learn from than descriptions:

  • The Five Dirtiest Tricks In Bullet Chess — Chess.com. "In Between Moves" and "Dirty Flagging" are the premove-busting sections.
  • Premove — Wikipedia. Covers the Rosen Trap: premoving into a deliberate stalemate.
  • Premove tricks in bullet — Lichess forum. Player-shared traps and counters.
Raise Premove rate toward 100% and lower Min confidence in the premove controls to make the bot premove more often and more exploitably.
